title: Operator Syntheses for Latency Spike Correspondence
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a pragmatic operator-oriented synthesis for investigating latency spikes that may span multiple layers (client, gateway, runtime, model sidecar, KV cache). The focus is on 'correspondence' — techniques that tie a visible latency spike to the minimal set of signals and reproducible artifacts required to triage and remediate.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: oncall engineers and SREs who need a compact reproducible path from alert to RCA.
- Scope: multi-tenant LLM inference flows, especially bursts where a subset of tenants see degraded P95/P99 but SLOs at aggregate appear nominal. Not a full instrumentation spec; this is an operator playbook + signal mapping.

High-level synthesis (quick read):
1) Establish a single session/sample: pick a representative request id or synthetic probe timestamp for the spike window.
2) Correlate these anchors across layers: client trace id -> gateway span -> routing decision -> model runtime span -> KV/cache spans -> backend calls (if any).
3) Extract minimal repro: same prompt length, same model variant, same tenant tags, same routing policy. Use synthetic replay harness with rate and concurrency knobs.
4) If repro fails, escalate to hypothesis tests: cold vs warm KV, quantization fallbacks, throttling/backpressure, model OOMs.

Signal taxonomy for correspondence (anchor-first approach):
- Anchor signals (always start here): probe_id, trace_id, request_id, tenant_id, model_name@version, route_tag, timestamp (ISO).
- Layer signals:
  * Client layer: observed RTT, client-side retry count, socket errors.
  * Gateway/proxy: route decision, chosen model variant, queue wait time, request size (tokens), priority flag.
  * Serving runtime: kernel-selection id, batch id, batch size, time-to-first-token, tail-kv-eviction, KV hit/miss (prefix & full), seq_len served, token_generation_ms per token.
  * Model sidecar: model load time, quantize-path, fallback-used boolean, GPU mem pressure, model crash/restart events.
  * Infra: node CPU%, GPU%/util, PCIe bandwd, host OOM events, network retries to object store.

Essential metric definitions (operator-facing):
- request_queue_wait_ms: time between gateway enqueue and dequeue (ms). Use p95/p99 slices.
- ttft_ms (time to first token): measure from gateway receive -> first token emitted from runtime. Prefer p50/p95/p99.
- token_gen_ms_per_token: total token generation time / token_count for the request. Useful for batch sizing regressions.
- kv_prefix_hit_rate: fraction of requests where prefix lookup succeeded. Important for multi-turn chat speedups.
- effective_batch_size: number of requests batched into a kernel execution (mean, p95).
- route_fallback_rate: fraction of requests that used fallback (cheaper model or serverless path).

Trace anchors and span design notes:
- Always include these tags on spans: trace_id, request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, batch_id, kv_cache_key (hashed), seed_prompt_hash (for privacy-safe repro).
- Add a per-span lightweight context dump (max 1KB): small JSON with {route, probe_id, token_count, seq_len, kernel_hint}. This is handier than chasing logs.
- Sampling policy: for latency anomalies, prefer deterministic sampling of the slowest N requests in the spike window (e.g., top 200 p99 events over 5m). Generic random sampling will hide correspondence.

Dashboard/Widget guidance (compact operators view):
- Spike ladder: small multi-panel strip ordered left->right: total requests per minute, p95 latency, ttft_p95, kv_prefix_hit_rate, effective_batch_size. Use same time range and aligned axes.
- Heatmap by tenant: x-axis time, y-axis top 30 tenants by traffic, color= p95 latency. Quick visual to find tenant-correlated spikes.
- Session playback widget: given an anchor id, show a compact timeline of spans and a link to the trace and raw request payload (if permitted).
- Batch composition inspector: histogram of batch_size during spike vs baseline. Helpful to detect batch growth that explains token-level regression.

Operator checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Pin the spike window (start/end) and capture top 5 highest-latency request ids.
2) For each id, fetch trace and verify presence of anchor tags. If trace missing, mark as 'trace-missing' and increase sampling rate.
3) Check KV hit/miss for each anchor. If a cluster of high-latency requests are KV misses, suspect cold-prefix regressions.
4) Inspect batch_id: are most slow requests grouped into a single oversized batch? If yes, temporarily limit max batch size and observe.
5) Check gateway route_fallback_rate: if elevated, some traffic might be using slow fallback models.
6) Check node-level metrics (GPU mem pressure, IO): if correlated, may be infra saturation.
7) Kick a synthetic replay with same token counts and tenant tags at 1x, 5x, 10x to see if latency reproduces.
8) If synthetic repro negative, mark hypothesis as 'non-repro' and capture artifacts for deeper analysis (kernel traces, perf counters).

Repro recipes (short):
- Cold-prefix repro: use probe with same token prefix, ensure KV cache is flushed for that tenant (use probe with unique tenant tag), then replay. Expect increased ttft and full-token generation time.
- Batch-race repro: simultaneously issue small-window burst of X requests to cause upstream batching algorithm to group them; observe effective_batch_size odor.
- Fallback-path repro: flip routing policy in staging to use same fallback and replay.

Quick queries / snippets (operator toolkit):
- Top slow request ids in window (SQL-ish pseudo):
  SELECT request_id, tenant_id, p95_latency_ms, kv_prefix_hit
  FROM requests
  WHERE ts BETWEEN '{{start}}' AND '{{end}}'
  ORDER BY p95_latency_ms DESC LIMIT 50;

- Batch composition:
  SELECT batch_id, COUNT(*) AS batch_size, avg(token_count)
  FROM runtime_batches
  WHERE ts BETWEEN '{{start}}' AND '{{end}}'
  GROUP BY batch_id ORDER BY batch_size DESC LIMIT 100;

- KV hit breakdown by tenant:
  SELECT tenant_id, SUM(kv_hits)/SUM(total_requests) AS kv_hit_rate
  FROM request_kv_stats
  WHERE ts between '{{start}}' and '{{end}}'
  GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY kv_hit_rate ASC LIMIT 50;

Debug artifacts to attach to postmortem:
- Representative trace ids (3–10).
- Kernel perf dumps for the spike window.
- Synthetic replay run id and configuration (payloads, concurrency).
- Node metrics snapshot (gpu/sysstat) and any kube eviction events.

Notes to self / unresolved questions (work-in-progress):
- Can we add a low-cardinality session fingerprint that preserves privacy but accelerates cross-layer joins? Idea: tenant-salt + prompt-hash truncated. Need privacy review.
- Pilot deterministic top-N trace capture on p99 events for 30 days and evaluate storage cost vs debugging speed.
- Is there a lightweight way to include sampled kernel-choice telemetry in gateway logs without blowing up cardinality? Maybe attach kernel_hint id only.

Action items (next 30 days):
- [ ] Add anchor tags enforcement to gateway and runtime (ownership: eng-serving-runtime).
- [ ] Dashboard: build spike ladder and session playback (ownership: eng-observability + UX).
- [ ] Experiment: enable deterministic p99 trace captures for 2 weeks (ownership: SRE).

Appendix: example incident vignette (condensed)
- Symptom: on 2026-01-08 14:03 UTC, tenant A saw p99 jump from 1.1s -> 4.5s for 12 minutes; aggregate p99 lightly increased.
- Anchor discovery: two trace ids showed KV miss cluster + oversized effective_batch_size=24.
- Root cause: batcher configuration regression from a recent change that permitted larger batching for long-context sessions; combined with KV eviction threshold being lowered during a separate deploy.
- Fix: roll back batcher config and revert KV eviction tuning; postmortem noted need for cross-feature rollout coordination.

If you're using this doc: please add your steps or small reproducible snippets beneath the "Notes to self" section and ping #obs-ops when you run a synthetic so we can build a replay library.

-- Rohit
